claim: The COVID-19 pandemic will likely take years to control globally.
source: The COVID-19 pandemic will likely take years to control globally, and constant epidemic surveillance will be required to limit the spread of SARS-CoV-2, especially considering the emergence of new variants that could hamper the effect of vaccination efforts.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the future trajectory of the pandemic based on current understanding.

claim: Constant epidemic surveillance will be required to limit the spread of SARS-CoV-2.
source: The COVID-19 pandemic will likely take years to control globally, and constant epidemic surveillance will be required to limit the spread of SARS-CoV-2, especially considering the emergence of new variants that could hamper the effect of vaccination efforts.
evidence: This is an inference based on epidemiological knowledge about disease control and the emergence of variants.

claim: New SARS-CoV-2 variants could hamper the effect of vaccination efforts.
source: The COVID-19 pandemic will likely take years to control globally, and constant epidemic surveillance will be required to limit the spread of SARS-CoV-2, especially considering the emergence of new variants that could hamper the effect of vaccination efforts.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of variants on vaccination, though based on scientific understanding.

claim: 81.3–100% of individuals with high-viral-load SARS-CoV-2 nasopharyngeal-positive samples also test positive for PoST.
source: We show that 81.3–100% of individuals with high-viral-load SARS-CoV-2 nasopharyngeal-positive samples also test positive for PoST, suggesting this method is effective in identifying COVID-19 contagious individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study comparing PoST results to nasopharyngeal RT-PCR results.

claim: PoST is effective in identifying COVID-19 contagious individuals.
source: We show that 81.3–100% of individuals with high-viral-load SARS-CoV-2 nasopharyngeal-positive samples also test positive for PoST, suggesting this method is effective in identifying COVID-19 contagious individuals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing high sensitivity of PoST for high viral load samples.

claim: Polymorphisms associated with SARS-CoV-2 Alpha, Beta, and Gamma variants were successfully identified in SARS-CoV-2-positive PoST samples.
source: Furthermore, we successfully identified polymorphisms associated with SARS-CoV-2 Alpha, Beta, and Gamma variants, in SARS-CoV-2-positive PoST samples.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR testing for specific variant-associated mutations.

claim: PoST is a non-invasive method for SARS-CoV-2 testing.
source: Overall, we report that PoST is a new non-invasive, cost-effective, and easy-to-implement smartphone-based smart alternative for SARS-CoV-2 testing, which could help to contain COVID-19 outbreaks and identification of variants of concern in the years to come.
evidence: This is based on the methodology described, which involves swabbing a smartphone screen rather than nasopharyngeal sampling.

claim: PoST is a cost-effective method for SARS-CoV-2 testing.
source: Overall, we report that PoST is a new non-invasive, cost-effective, and easy-to-implement smartphone-based smart alternative for SARS-CoV-2 testing, which could help to contain COVID-19 outbreaks and identification of variants of concern in the years to come.
evidence: This is supported by data comparing costs of PoST to nasopharyngeal testing described in the Discussion section.

claim: PoST is an easy-to-implement method for SARS-CoV-2 testing.
source: Overall, we report that PoST is a new non-invasive, cost-effective, and easy-to-implement smartphone-based smart alternative for SARS-CoV-2 testing, which could help to contain COVID-19 outbreaks and identification of variants of concern in the years to come.
evidence: This is based on the methodology and discussion of implementation requirements.

claim: PoST could help to contain COVID-19 outbreaks.
source: Overall, we report that PoST is a new non-invasive, cost-effective, and easy-to-implement smartphone-based smart alternative for SARS-CoV-2 testing, which could help to contain COVID-19 outbreaks and identification of variants of concern in the years to come.

claim: PoST could help with identification of variants of concern.

evidence: This is supported by data showing successful variant identification in PoST samples.

claim: The Alpha variant (B.1.1.7) is more infectious.
source: Particularly, the more infectious Alpha variant (B.1.1.7, Frampton et al., 2021; Rambaut et al., 2020), together with the Beta variant (B.1.351, Tegally et al., 2020), Delta (B.1617.2, Torjesen, 2021) and Gamma variant (P.1, Faria et al., 2021 ), considered variants of concern by CDC, which share the antigenic drift and/or signature mutations E484K, L452R,K417N and N501Y in the region of the spike protein that is recognised by neutralising antibodies (Collier et al., 2021; Tchesnokova et al., 2021; Greaney et al., 2021b; Wang et al., 2021; Wibmer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on the Alpha variant.

claim: Alpha, Beta, Delta, and Gamma variants are considered variants of concern by CDC.
source: Particularly, the more infectious Alpha variant (B.1.1.7, Frampton et al., 2021; Rambaut et al., 2020), together with the Beta variant (B.1.351, Tegally et al., 2020), Delta (B.1617.2, Torjesen, 2021) and Gamma variant (P.1, Faria et al., 2021 ), considered variants of concern by CDC, which share the antigenic drift and/or signature mutations E484K, L452R,K417N and N501Y in the region of the spike protein that is recognised by neutralising antibodies (Collier et al., 2021; Tchesnokova et al., 2021; Greaney et al., 2021b; Wang et al., 2021; Wibmer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from CDC classification.

claim: Alpha, Beta, Delta, and Gamma variants share signature mutations E484K, L452R, K417N and N501Y in the spike protein region recognised by neutralising antibodies.
source: Particularly, the more infectious Alpha variant (B.1.1.7, Frampton et al., 2021; Rambaut et al., 2020), together with the Beta variant (B.1.351, Tegally et al., 2020), Delta (B.1617.2, Torjesen, 2021) and Gamma variant (P.1, Faria et al., 2021 ), considered variants of concern by CDC, which share the antigenic drift and/or signature mutations E484K, L452R,K417N and N501Y in the region of the spike protein that is recognised by neutralising antibodies (Collier et al., 2021; Tchesnokova et al., 2021; Greaney et al., 2021b; Wang et al., 2021; Wibmer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research on variant mutations.

claim: The RNA sequence of SARS-CoV-2 was made available early in the pandemic.
source: Early in the pandemic, the RNA sequence of the SARS-CoV-2 virus was made available (Wu et al., 2020), enabling the testing of infected patients by reverse transcription (RT)–PCR (Arnaout et al., 2020; Corman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2020.

claim: The availability of SARS-CoV-2 RNA sequence enabled testing of infected patients by RT-PCR.
source: Early in the pandemic, the RNA sequence of the SARS-CoV-2 virus was made available (Wu et al., 2020), enabling the testing of infected patients by reverse transcription (RT)–PCR (Arnaout et al., 2020; Corman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on RT-PCR testing methods.

claim: Many infected individuals express no symptoms, inadvertently spreading the infection.
source: Regular and broad testing of SARS-CoV-2 seems essential to contain the propagation of SARS-CoV-2, as many infected individuals express no symptoms, inadvertently spreading the infection (Ferretti et al., 2020; Kronbichler et al., 2020; Petersen and Phillips, 2020; Pollock and Lancaster, 2020; Sayampanathan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research on asymptomatic transmission.

claim: Regular and broad testing of SARS-CoV-2 is essential to contain the propagation of SARS-CoV-2.
source: Regular and broad testing of SARS-CoV-2 seems essential to contain the propagation of SARS-CoV-2, as many infected individuals express no symptoms, inadvertently spreading the infection (Ferretti et al., 2020; Kronbichler et al., 2020; Petersen and Phillips, 2020; Pollock and Lancaster, 2020; Sayampanathan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited research about asymptomatic transmission and epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Successful epidemiological surveillance strategies should include large-scale screening methods that enable periodic and continuous testing of the general population.
source: Therefore, successful epidemiological surveillance strategies required to monitor the spread of SARS-CoV-2 and the outbreak of new strains should include large-scale screening methods that enable periodic and continuous testing of the general population.
evidence: This is an inference based on epidemiological knowledge and the need to monitor virus spread.

claim: Testing capacity has been limited, hampering attempts to control the spread of SARS-CoV-2.
source: However, testing capacity has been limited, hampering attempts to control the spread of SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about pandemic response challenges.

claim: Reliable nasopharyngeal sampling and RT-PCR testing is highly invasive.
source: One obstacle is that reliable nasopharyngeal sampling and RT-PCR testing is highly invasive and requires both specialised staff and appropriate conditions for the manipulation and transport of the samples to comply with clinical standards and protocols expected by regulatory bodies (CDC, 2021b; UK-Government U, 2021).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about nasopharyngeal sampling procedures.

claim: Nasopharyngeal sampling and RT-PCR testing requires specialised staff.
source: One obstacle is that reliable nasopharyngeal sampling and RT-PCR testing is highly invasive and requires both specialised staff and appropriate conditions for the manipulation and transport of the samples to comply with clinical standards and protocols expected by regulatory bodies (CDC, 2021b; UK-Government U, 2021).

claim: Nasopharyngeal sampling and RT-PCR testing requires appropriate conditions for sample manipulation and transport to comply with clinical standards.

claim: Lateral flow device antigen tests are cheaper than RT-PCR tests.
source: Lateral flow device antigen tests are cheaper, accurate when detecting individuals with high viral load, and an epidemiologically effective option to identify SARS-CoV-2 contagious people (Dinnes et al., 2021; Pavelka et al., 2021; Wagenhäuser et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on lateral flow tests.

claim: Lateral flow device antigen tests are accurate when detecting individuals with high viral load.
source: Lateral flow device antigen tests are cheaper, accurate when detecting individuals with high viral load, and an epidemiologically effective option to identify SARS-CoV-2 contagious people (Dinnes et al., 2021; Pavelka et al., 2021; Wagenhäuser et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on lateral flow test accuracy.

claim: Lateral flow device antigen tests are an epidemiologically effective option to identify SARS-CoV-2 contagious people.
source: Lateral flow device antigen tests are cheaper, accurate when detecting individuals with high viral load, and an epidemiologically effective option to identify SARS-CoV-2 contagious people (Dinnes et al., 2021; Pavelka et al., 2021; Wagenhäuser et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on lateral flow test effectiveness.

claim: Lateral flow device antigen tests require nasopharyngeal sampling.
source: Yet, correct testing also requires nasopharyngeal sampling.

claim: Regular large-scale testing is difficult because accurate tests are either too invasive, expensive, or logistically complicated to implement.
source: Therefore, regular large-scale testing is difficult because accurate tests are either too invasive, expensive, or logistically complicated to implement, which make them unviable for the task.
evidence: This is an inference based on the described limitations of existing testing methods.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 RNA can be detected from many different kinds of surfaces, places, and devices, including phones.
source: SARS-CoV-2 RNA can be detected from many different kinds of surfaces, places, and devices, including phones (Marshall et al., 2020; Santarpia et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research on SARS-CoV-2 surface detection.

claim: Active SARS-CoV-2 virus is more likely to be recovered from some surfaces when expelled from individuals with seemingly high viral load.
source: Furthermore, active SARS-CoV-2 virus is more likely to be recovered from some surfaces when expelled from individuals with seemingly high viral load (Bullard et al., 2020; Jefferson et al., 2020; Sonnleitner et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on viral recovery from surfaces.

claim: Smartphones are personal objects that are constantly exposed to peoples' mouths.
source: Smartphones are personal objects that are constantly exposed to peoples' mouths, their screens becoming a likely contaminated surface.

claim: Smartphone screens become a likely contaminated surface.
source: Smartphones are personal objects that are constantly exposed to peoples' mouths, their screens becoming a likely contaminated surface.

claim: COVID-19 contagious individuals will regularly deposit aerosols, droplets of saliva, or upper respiratory tract secretions containing shed SARS-CoV-2 virions over the screen of their phone.
source: Therefore, we hypothesised that COVID-19 contagious individuals will regularly deposit aerosols, droplets of saliva, or upper respiratory tract secretions containing shed SARS-CoV-2 virions, over the screen of their phone, which could then be sampled and detected by RT-PCR.
evidence: This is the hypothesis being tested in the study, based on inference from known transmission mechanisms.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 virions deposited on phone screens can be sampled and detected by RT-PCR.
source: Therefore, we hypothesised that COVID-19 contagious individuals will regularly deposit aerosols, droplets of saliva, or upper respiratory tract secretions containing shed SARS-CoV-2 virions, over the screen of their phone, which could then be sampled and detected by RT-PCR.

claim: The pilot cohort consisted of both symptomatic and asymptomatic or pre-symptomatic individuals.
source: The cohort sample in this pilot study consisted of both symptomatic and asymptomatic or pre-symptomatic individuals who required SARS-CoV-2 testing due to a suspected SARS-CoV-2 infection, close contact to SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals, or return to work and travel authorisation requests in Santiago, Chile, between September and October 2020 (3.81% ± 1.0 average positivity rate in Santiago, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This describes the study cohort composition based on the study design.

claim: The pilot study was conducted in Santiago, Chile, between September and October 2020.
source: The cohort sample in this pilot study consisted of both symptomatic and asymptomatic or pre-symptomatic individuals who required SARS-CoV-2 testing due to a suspected SARS-CoV-2 infection, close contact to SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals, or return to work and travel authorisation requests in Santiago, Chile, between September and October 2020 (3.81% ± 1.0 average positivity rate in Santiago, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is factual information about when and where the study was conducted.

claim: Santiago had a 3.81% ± 1.0 average positivity rate during September and October 2020.
source: The cohort sample in this pilot study consisted of both symptomatic and asymptomatic or pre-symptomatic individuals who required SARS-CoV-2 testing due to a suspected SARS-CoV-2 infection, close contact to SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals, or return to work and travel authorisation requests in Santiago, Chile, between September and October 2020 (3.81% ± 1.0 average positivity rate in Santiago, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).

claim: Of 540 individuals in the pilot study, 51 tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by nasopharyngeal RT-PCR detection.

claim: All samples with Ct value under 20 also tested positive for PoST (n = 15).

claim: The sensitivity of PoST is 100% in individuals with high viral load (Ct value under 20).
source: Our results suggest that the ability for PoST to correctly identify positive nasopharyngeal individuals, sensitivity, is 100% in individuals with high viral load, Ct value under 20.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing all low Ct samples were PoST positive.

claim: The accumulated sensitivity of PoST in nasopharyngeal samples with medium Ct values below 30 is 89.7% (n = 29).
source: As shown in Figure 1C (red line, Source data 1), the accumulated sensitivity of PoST in nasopharyngeal samples with medium Ct values below 30 is 89.7% (n = 29, medium and low viral load).

claim: Testing samples from smartphone screens is effective in identifying COVID-19-positive patients with low and medium Ct RT-PCR result values.
source: Therefore, our results suggest that testing samples from smartphone screens is effective in identifying COVID-19-positive patients with low and medium Ct RT-PCR result values, which are thought to be actively contagious and expelling virus particles (Bullard et al., 2020; Jefferson et al., 2020; Sonnleitner et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing high sensitivity at low and medium Ct values.

claim: Patients with low and medium Ct RT-PCR result values are thought to be actively contagious and expelling virus particles.
source: Therefore, our results suggest that testing samples from smartphone screens is effective in identifying COVID-19-positive patients with low and medium Ct RT-PCR result values, which are thought to be actively contagious and expelling virus particles (Bullard et al., 2020; Jefferson et al., 2020; Sonnleitner et al., 2021).

source: Of all the PoST and nasopharyngeal-positive samples in this cohort, 76% (n = 22/29) corresponded to individuals with no specific COVID-19 symptoms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Source data 1).

claim: Testing smartphone screens is effective in identifying COVID-19-infected individuals regardless of their symptoms at the time of testing.

claim: Two of the PoST-positive/nasopharyngeal-negative cases had three clear COVID-19 symptoms.

claim: Some PoST-positive/nasopharyngeal-negative cases could be nasopharyngeal false-negative results rather than PoST false positives.

claim: The Ct values from the pilot cohort showed an apparent bimodal distribution.

claim: Over seven thousand SARS-CoV-2-positive samples from Davila Clinic were analyzed.

claim: The Ct value distribution from the Davila Clinic dataset was consistent with the pilot data at the months the pilot cohort was tested.

claim: It is unlikely that PoST-positive results in high Ct value samples are due to detection of long-lasting virus or RNA on the phone screen surface.
source: Given the unstable nature of the SARS-CoV-2 virus on surfaces (Goldman, 2020), and the pervasive activity of RNases that are ubiquitously present in the environment (Probst et al., 2006), it is unlikely that these positive PoST results are due to the detection of long-lasting virus or RNA on the phone screen surface.

source: Hence, we could exclude the possibility that these PoST-positive results are the consequence of detecting RNA from when individuals were passing through a moment of higher COVID-19 infection. Therefore, one could speculate that these results are the consequence of suboptimal nasopharyngeal sampling, which would explain the low amount of virus in the sample and hence, a high Ct value.

claim: It is plausible that some PoST-positive/high Ct nasopharyngeal samples belong to individuals with low viral load that are still actively contagious.
